title: Three strangers at Mamre (Genesis 18:1–15)
hook: Abraham runs to feed three visitors, and Sarah laughs behind the tent

segments.voice: Yesterday, El Roi, the God who sees, the name Hagar gave at a spring, and your line was you are seen. Whose name did you learn and use? Day three hundred fifty-three.

The hottest part of the day, in the hill country near Hebron. Nobody travels at noon if they can help it. Abraham, with the new name God has given him, is sitting at the door of his tent by the great trees of Mamre. He's ninety-nine years old. He looks up, and there are three men standing near him. Strangers. No warning, no dust cloud on the road. Just there. What he does next turns a hot afternoon into a feast.
screen: `NOON, IN THE HEAT OF THE DAY.` → `NINETY-NINE, AT THE TENT DOOR.` → `THREE STRANGERS, JUST THERE.`

segments.voice: He runs. A ninety-nine-year-old man, in the heat, runs to meet them and bows to the ground. And then listen to how modest his offer is, in the King James Bible: "Let a little water, I pray you, be fetched, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree: And I will fetch a morsel of bread." A little water, a morsel of bread. And then he hurries. He tells Sarah to make cakes from a huge amount of fine flour. He runs to the herd for a tender calf. Butter, milk, meat. A morsel turns into a feast, and he stands by them under the tree while they eat. Then one of them asks: where is Sarah thy wife? And promises that by this time next year, Sarah will have a son. Sarah is listening behind the tent door. She's around ninety. And she laughs, quietly, to herself: worn out as I am, and my husband old, shall I have this pleasure now? The visitor hears it. Why did Sarah laugh? And then the question at the center of today: "Is any thing too hard for the LORD?" In Hebrew, too hard is too wonderful, from the word pele, a wonder, beyond reach. Sarah, afraid, says I didn't laugh. The answer: "Nay; but thou didst laugh." Who are these three? The text moves between three men and the LORD speaking. Some Christian readers have seen a hint of the Trinity here; Andrei Rublev's Orthodox icon paints the three seated around one table. Jewish tradition reads the three as angels, with God appearing to Abraham. And the New Testament letter to the Hebrews draws its own lesson: some have entertained angels unawares.
screen: `A NINETY-NINE-YEAR-OLD RUNS.` · `A MORSEL BECOMES A FEAST.` · `SARAH LAUGHS BEHIND THE TENT.` · `WHO ARE THE THREE?` · then, large: `IS ANY THING TOO HARD FOR THE LORD?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome a visitor properly. Settle, and breathe. Think of the next person who'll come to your door, your desk, your table: a friend, a delivery driver, a coworker, a kid's friend. Picture them arriving. Now picture Abraham's way: getting up, going to meet them, offering water before they ask, something to eat, a place to sit. Small, but more than they expect. Notice what you'd usually do instead. If you pray, you can pray for whoever comes next. The bell holds the time.
Pele. Hebrew for a wonder, beyond reach, as in is anything too wonderful for the Lord: the promise Sarah laughed to hear, too wonderful to believe.
Your line: is anything too hard? Today, when someone comes to you, get up and offer something first: water, a seat, your full attention. Day three hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Hospitality to strangers is a long Christian practice, from monasteries that receive every guest as Christ to churches that run open tables, and Rublev's icon of the three visitors hangs in many Orthodox homes and churches.

what it means: a ninety-nine-year-old runs to feed strangers, and hears a promise too wonderful to believe.
what a scholar hears: too hard is from pele, wonder; the text moves between three men and the LORD; Rublev's icon and Hebrews 13:2 both grow from this tent door.

notes: Abraham's age 99 (17:24, 'the selfsame day' context) and Sarah about 90 (17:17). Confirm.
Name changes Abram→Abraham, Sarai→Sarah happen in Genesis 17, which the path does not teach as its own day; mentioned in passing. Keeper may wish a fuller note.
'Too hard' = yippale, from the root p-l-', 'wonder' (pele). Confirm.
Rublev's Trinity icon (c. 1410s–1420s). Confirm; 'many Christians have seen a hint of the Trinity' and Jewish readings ('God appearing with angels') stated fairly.
Hebrews 13:2 paraphrased ('some have entertained angels unawares'); confirm.
